title: James VI's Daemonologie: Royal Endorsement of Witch Prosecution
description: King James VI of Scotland published Daemonologie in Edinburgh in 1597, a systematic demonological treatise written as a dialogue refuting Weyer and Scot and endorsing the reality of witchcraft and the necessity of prosecution. James drew directly on his experience at the North Berwick trials and on continental demonological literature to produce an accessible vernacular summary of witch-theory. When James became James I of England in 1603, Daemonologie was reprinted in London, he reportedly ordered Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft burned, and within a year he had secured passage of the harsher 1604 Witchcraft Act. No European monarch so directly shaped witch-prosecution legislation through personal engagement with demonological theory.
historiographical_note: Stuart Clark in Thinking with Demons analyzes Daemonologie as serious theology, not mere royal superstition. James's arguments engage substantively with Weyer and Scot and reflect genuine engagement with demonological debate. Later scholars have noted, however, that James's enthusiasm for witch prosecution waned significantly after 1616, when several cases were exposed as fraudulent — suggesting his belief was more conditional than Daemonologie implies.
source_method: James VI, Daemonologie (1597); Clark, Thinking with Demons (1997); Normand and Roberts, Witchcraft in Early Modern Scotland (2000)
